draft.title: Living through environmental change
card: The last ice age ended about 18,000 to 7,000 years ago. The climate warmed, ice melted and sea levels rose.
Rising seas flooded low land. Tasmania was cut off from the mainland, and the Torres Strait Islands formed from land that had once joined Australia to New Guinea.
Many very large animals, called megafauna, died out. Inland lakes also dried up as the climate changed.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples lived through these changes. They adapted how and where they lived, using new food sources and moving to new places.
draft.remember: Warming and rising seas reshaped the land, and people adapted to the change.

a.q: What happened to the sea as the last ice age ended?
opts: Ice melted and sea levels rose, cutting off Tasmania
Ice grew and sea levels fell, so Tasmania joined up
Sea levels stayed the same, but lakes filled with water
Sea levels rose, so the Torres Strait Islands joined up
a.why: As the climate warmed, ice melted and the sea rose, which cut Tasmania off from the mainland. The last option has it backwards: rising seas separated the islands from the mainland and from New Guinea.
a.clue: Think about what warming does to ice.

b.q: A teacher says that people living on a lake shore in inland Australia watched it dry up as the ice age ended. Which response best fits what the people did?
opts: They adapted by changing where they lived and what they ate
They stayed by the dry lake and kept exactly the same life
They left Australia, because the whole land had dried out
They stopped living in the area, as megafauna had died out
b.why: People lived through change by adapting how and where they lived, such as moving and using other food. The tempting option, staying with an unchanged life, ignores the adapting that the card describes.
b.clue: The card says people changed how and where they lived.

a.best: Ice melted and sea levels rose, cutting off Tasmania

b.best: They adapted by changing where they lived and what they ate

problems.detail: The card places the megafauna extinction among the changes at the end of the last ice age (18,000 to 7,000 years ago). Most Australian megafauna died out much earlier, around 45,000 to 40,000 years ago, before the Last Glacial Maximum. The chapter outline for this point repeats the same framing.
The clue ('The card says people changed how and where they lived') restates the right option almost word for word, so a student can pick it without thinking about the scenario.

Why (a) refers to 'the last option', but the options appear in a random order. It also explains the Torres Strait error ('rising seas separated the islands... from New Guinea') while seeming to describe the 'Ice grew and sea levels fell' option, which is confusing.

check.summary: The card wrongly presents the megafauna extinction as part of the end of the last ice age, when most Australian megafauna died out around 45,000 to 40,000 years ago. Question b's clue gives the answer away, and why (a) refers to an option by position and mixes up which wrong option it is explaining.

proposal.title: Living through environmental change
card: The coldest part of the last ice age was about 20,000 years ago. After that the climate warmed, ice melted and sea levels rose until about 7,000 years ago.
Rising seas flooded low land. Tasmania was cut off from the mainland, and the Torres Strait Islands formed from high ground on land that had once joined Australia to New Guinea.
As the climate changed, many inland lakes dried up. Megafauna, very large animals such as giant kangaroos, had mostly died out much earlier, tens of thousands of years before the seas rose.
Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples lived through these changes. They adapted how and where they lived, using new food sources and moving to new places.
proposal.remember: Warming and rising seas reshaped the land, and people adapted how and where they lived.

a.q: What happened to the sea as the last ice age ended?
opts: Sea levels rose and cut Tasmania off from the mainland
Sea levels fell and joined Tasmania to the mainland
Sea levels rose and joined New Guinea to Australia
Sea levels stayed the same while inland lakes filled
a.why: As the climate warmed, ice melted and the sea rose, flooding the low land between Tasmania and the mainland. The option saying the sea joined New Guinea to Australia has it backwards: rising seas flooded the land between them, leaving only the Torres Strait Islands above water.
a.clue: Think about what warming does to ice, and where that water goes.

b.q: People lived beside an inland lake that slowly dried up as the climate changed. Which response best fits what people did in times like this?
opts: They moved to other places and used different food sources
They hunted megafauna in place of food from the lake
They left the continent, because all of Australia dried out
They stayed on the dry shore and kept their old way of life
b.why: When a place changed, people adapted by moving and finding other foods. Hunting megafauna is tempting, but most megafauna had died out tens of thousands of years before this time, so they were not there to hunt.
b.clue: Once the water was gone, what would people need to find?
